html:
The Viking Age was the period, roughly 793 to 1066, when Norse people from Scandinavia raided, traded and settled across Europe and the North Atlantic. Its usual bookends are the raid on the monastery of Lindisfarne in England and the battle of Stamford Bridge.

At home most Scandinavians were farmers, living in a world of chieftains, assemblies called things, and old gods such as Odin and Thor. What set them apart were their ships: long, shallow and fast, able to cross open sea and row far up rivers.

Where they went:

  • West: raids on Britain, Ireland and France; the Danelaw in England; a duchy in Normandy, whose dukes later made the Norman conquest of England.
  • North Atlantic: the settlement of Iceland from about 874, then Greenland, and a short stay in North America at L'Anse aux Meadows around 1021.
  • East: Swedes known as Varangians went down Russian rivers to the Black and Caspian seas. They helped found Kievan Rus', and served the Byzantine emperor in the Varangian Guard.

Raiding was only part of it. Vikings carried slaves, furs and Arab silver along their trade routes, and silver coins from the Islamic world turn up in large hoards in Sweden.

The age ended as Scandinavia became Christian and its kingdoms, Denmark, Norway and Sweden, took firm shape under kings who ruled more like those elsewhere in Europe. Harald Hardrada's death at Stamford Bridge in 1066 is the conventional end.
